title: Code Review Basics
description: Review a small function that a teammate wrote and decide if it is ready to merge.

exercise.task: Your teammate Lisa wrote a function that calculates the average grade of a student. The code runs without errors. Review her pull request.
requirements: Returns the average of all grades in the list
Returns 0 when the list is empty
Does not change the original list

look: Go through the requirements one by one and find the line that handles each one.
Check where loops start and stop.
Run the example input in your head. Do you get 8?
Think about edge cases, like an empty list.
write: Point to the exact line you mean.
Explain why it is a problem, not only what to change.
Suggest a fix or ask a question.
Talk about the code, not about the person.

issues.title: The loop skips the first grade
issues.wrong: The loop starts at i = 1, so grades[0] is never added to the sum.
issues.why: Every average is wrong. With [6, 8, 10] the function returns 6 instead of 8. Because the code runs without errors, this bug is easy to miss.
issues.improve: Start the loop at i = 0, or use a for...of loop so you cannot pick the wrong index.

issues.title: An empty list returns NaN
issues.wrong: When grades is empty, the function calculates 0 / 0, which is NaN.
issues.why: The requirement says an empty list should return 0. NaN spreads through every calculation that uses it, so the bug shows up somewhere else.
issues.improve: Return 0 early when the list is empty, before dividing.

expert.summary: Thanks Lisa, the function is short and easy to follow! Two requirements are not met yet, so I am requesting changes.

comments.text: The loop starts at i = 1, so the first grade is never added. With [6, 8, 10] this returns 6 instead of 8. Could we start at i = 0?
For an empty list this divides 0 by 0 and returns NaN, but the requirement says it should return 0. Maybe add an early return when the list is empty?

why: Each comment points to one specific line.
It explains the impact with a concrete example.
Fixes are suggested as questions, which keeps the tone friendly.
It requests changes because the requirements are not met.

title: Naming & Readability
description: This code works, but is it easy for your team to read and change?
learn: Give feedback on code that already works

exercise.task: Your teammate Tom wrote a function that checks whether a student passed a course. All tests pass. Review his pull request.
requirements: Students pass with a grade of 5.5 or higher
Students must attend at least 80% of the 20 lessons
Teammates should understand the code without asking Tom

look: The code works, so look past whether it is correct.
Would a new teammate understand every name?
Look for numbers without an explanation.
write: Explain what was confusing for you as a reader.
Suggest a better name instead of only saying it is bad.
Keep the tone friendly. Working code is already a good start.

issues.title: Names do not explain what they mean
issues.wrong: check, s, g and a do not say what the function does or what the values are.
issues.why: Teammates have to read the whole function (or ask Tom) to understand it. Unclear names slow down every future review and change.
issues.improve: Use names that describe the meaning, like hasPassed(student), student.grade and student.attendance.

issues.title: Magic number 20
issues.wrong: 20 is the number of lessons, but the code does not say so.
issues.why: If the course gets more lessons, someone has to find and change this hidden number. It is easy to forget.
issues.improve: Move it into a named constant like TOTAL_LESSONS, or pass the number of lessons in.

expert.summary: Nice work, Tom. The logic is correct! A few small readability changes will make this much easier for the rest of us.

comments.text: I had to read the whole function to see what check, s, g and a mean. Could we rename them to hasPassed(student), grade and attendance?
Is 20 the number of lessons? If the course length changes this breaks silently. Could we move it into a constant like TOTAL_LESSONS?

why: It starts with something positive: the logic is correct.
It explains the problem from the reader's point of view.
It suggests concrete names instead of only saying they are bad.
It requests changes because readability is one of the requirements.

title: Testing Edge Cases
description: Tests that pass are not always good tests. Find what these tests forget.
learn: Check whether a test expects the right result

exercise.task: Your teammate Noor wrote tests for isValidPassword(password). The test run is green. Review the tests in her pull request.
requirements: A valid password has at least 8 characters
A valid password contains at least one number
The tests check both valid and invalid passwords

look: Read each test name, then check if the expectation matches it.
List every requirement and look for a test that covers it.
A green test run does not mean the tests are correct.
write: Name the requirement that is not tested.
Explain what could go wrong in production.

issues.title: The short-password test expects true
issues.wrong: The test is called "rejects a short password" but it expects true.
issues.why: This test passes when the function is broken and fails when it is correct. It gives the team false confidence.
issues.improve: Expect false for a short password.

issues.title: No test for a password without a number
issues.wrong: None of the tests check the "at least one number" requirement.
issues.why: If someone breaks the number check, every test stays green and the bug reaches users.
issues.improve: Add a test with a long password without numbers that expects false.
issues.fix: test("rejects a password without a number", () => {

expert.summary: Thanks Noor! Good test names, they make the intent very clear. One expectation is flipped and one requirement is not covered yet.

comments.text: This test is called "rejects a short password" but it expects true, so it passes when the function is broken. Should this be toBe(false)?
I could not find a test for the "at least one number" rule. Could we add one, for example isValidPassword("frogyfrogy") should be false?

why: It praises the clear test names first.
It explains the risk: a green run that hides a broken function.
It gives a concrete example test the author can copy.
It requests changes because the tests can hide real bugs.
